source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Expected value of perfect information
finding: EVPI is the price one would pay for perfect information. EVPI = EV with perfect information minus expected value of the best action now (EMV).
numbers: EMV = max_i sum_j p_j R_ij. EV|PI = sum_j p_j max_i R_ij. EVPI = EV|PI - EMV.
limits: Textbook form; assumes risk neutrality, a known payoff table and known priors.
agent_relevance: S4/S7: before running a test, compute the most any test could be worth. If the test costs more than EVPI, skip it.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Expected value of perfect information, worked example
finding: Investment example: knowing the market direction in advance is worth 350.
limits: Toy textbook example (Hubbard 2007 cited); not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Use as a unit test for the agent's EVPI routine: it must return 350.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Expected value of perfect information, properties
finding: EVPI is never negative, because the decision maker can ignore the information. No information-gathering act can be worth more than EVPI. With two choices and two outcomes, EVPI cannot exceed half the largest reward difference between the choices under either outcome.
numbers: 0 <= value of any test <= EVPI. Two-choice two-outcome bound = 0.5 * max reward gap.
quote: No other information-gathering activity can be worth more
limits: The page states EVPI as an upper bound; it gives no proof.
agent_relevance: Cheap guard: a test that costs more than EVPI is never worth running, whatever its accuracy.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Value of information
finding: Value of information equals value of the decision situation with perfect information minus value of the current one (risk neutral). It is never negative. The value of imperfect information about one variable can equal the value of perfect information about a related one. Values of two pieces of evidence are not additive; the second is valued after updating on the first. The order of observation does not change the total gain in maximum expected utility. Source named: Howard (1966), IEEE Trans. Systems Science and Cybernetics 2(1), 22-26.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Risk-averse or risk-seeking agents need iterative computation; the simple subtraction fails.
agent_relevance: Choose tests one at a time and re-compute value after each result; never add two test values together.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Value of information, consultant model
finding: Symbolic model of hiring an expert at cost c. Without information E = g*k + (1-g)*k'. With a perfect consultant F = g*(k+c). Hire when F < E. An imperfect consultant with error rate f and a correction cost m gives a recursive formula.
numbers: E = gk+(1-g)k'. F = g(k+c). Recursive: E = gk+(1-g)(k'+m+E). Imperfect: F = g(k+c)(1-f)+g(k+c+F)f+(1-g)(1-f)(k+c+F)+(1-g)f(k'+c+m+F).
limits: No numeric examples on the page. Formulas copied as stated, not re-derived.
agent_relevance: Shows an unreliable test (error rate f) can be priced; fits a check-and-retry loop in the agent.

source: Howard (1966) Information value theory. IEEE Trans. Systems Science and Cybernetics 2(1):22-26
finding: Founding paper that names the expected value of perfect information (clairvoyance) as the most a decision maker should pay to learn an uncertainty. Known here only through citations (Wikipedia, Hay et al. 2012). The paper itself was not opened; an attempt to fetch the IEEE page returned no content.
numbers: Pages 22-26 (from Wikipedia reference). No figures verified.
limits: Not read. Everything attributed to it is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Cite as the origin of the EVPI bound; do not quote numbers from it.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications (UAI)
finding: Traces the idea that computations can be chosen by their expected improvement in decision quality. Matheson (1968) borrowed it from Howard (1966). I. J. Good (1968) proposed it to control chess search and defined Type II rationality. Russell and Wefald (1988, 1991) built a metalevel sequential model and applied it to Othello. Hay et al. recast the problem as Bayesian selection.
numbers: Dates: Howard 1966, Matheson 1968, Good 1968, Russell and Wefald 1988/1991.
limits: History as told by the paper's own authors.
agent_relevance: Gives the lineage of value of computation as value of information applied to thinking steps (S4/S7).

source: Hay et al. (2012) Theorem 5, bound on number of computations
finding: The optimal policy's expected number of computations is bounded by the value of perfect information times 1/c, where c is the cost per computation. A policy with infinite expected computations has value minus infinity, so the optimal policy stops with probability one.
numbers: E[number of computations] <= EVPI / c.
quote: bounded by the value of perfect information
limits: Assumes a fixed cost per computation c > 0 (the paper cites Harada 1997 for when that holds) and utilities bounded in [0,1].
agent_relevance: Direct budget rule: cap the number of test or thinking steps near EVPI/c. A higher cost per step shrinks the cap.

source: Hay et al. (2012) Theorem 10, one-armed Bernoulli bound
finding: For the one-armed Bernoulli metalevel problem the optimal policy performs at most about 1/(4c) - 3 computations, so the optimal policy can be computed in time O(1/c^2).
numbers: Bound <= 1/(4c) - 3, because the maximum of mu(1-mu) is 1/4. Our arithmetic: c=0.001 gives at most 247 samples.
limits: Proven only for the one-armed Bernoulli model with beta posteriors. The extracted text of the first bound form was garbled; the 1/(4c)-3 form is the one legible in the paper.
agent_relevance: Shows that a finite stopping rule exists even for open-ended testing.

source: Hay et al. (2012) myopic, blinkered and non-indexable policies
finding: The myopic policy (one-step value of information) stops too early because changing one's mind often takes several computations. A blinkered policy looks several steps along one arm and beats myopic. Optimal metalevel policies are not index policies: the best computation can flip between arms as the context value changes. UCT, a bandit rule used in Go, applies bandit theory to a problem that is not a bandit problem, because simulations cost the same whatever the utility of the action simulated.
numbers: Theorem 7: if the myopic policy continues, the optimal policy does too. Figure 1: optimal choice flips from observing arm 1 to arm 2 as the fixed alternative's value varies. Flat-selection comparison used k=25 arms.
limits: Selection-problem model; real tool calls have uneven costs and dependent outcomes.
agent_relevance: Do not stop a test sequence just because the next single test has near-zero value; check a bundle of 2-3 tests before concluding stop.

source: Hay et al. (2012) Go experiment with VOI-based stopping
finding: A sampler that used value of information to stop and to allocate samples beat the strong UCT player Pachi on 9x9 Go, with the gain largest at middling sample budgets.
numbers: Win rate 64% against UCT at 10000 samples per ply with stopping threshold c=1e-6. Budgets tested: 5000, 7000, 10000, 15000 samples per ply. Each experiment repeated 1000 times.
limits: 9x9 board only; the UCT engine is not Pachi's strongest. Pachi's sample reuse favoured the baseline; without reuse the VOI scheme did better. Win rates for other budgets were read from a plot only.
agent_relevance: Hard evidence that choosing computations by value per cost beats a fixed plan in a search task.

source: Hay et al. (2012) Example 3, unbounded-length counterexample
finding: The optimal policy need not decide in bounded time: with a sequential-probability-ratio-type prior it can keep sampling, with exponentially shrinking but positive chance of arbitrarily long runs, yet it stops with probability one.
numbers: Two arms, arm 1 constant 1/2, arm 2 is 1/3 or 2/3 with equal probability. Posterior odds are 2^(s-f). With probability 1/3 a state with s-f=0 returns to s-f=0 after two samples.
limits: Constructed example, not an empirical result.
agent_relevance: A hard cap on tests is still needed even though theory says stopping is certain.

source: Rainforth, Foster, Ivanova, Bickford Smith (2024) Modern Bayesian Experimental Design (Statistical Science)
finding: Bayesian experimental design picks the experiment that maximises the expected utility of the data. The standard utility is expected information gain (EIG), the expected reduction in Shannon entropy of the quantity of interest. Lindley (1956) is the origin. Defining EIG only needs a way to simulate (theta, y) pairs.
numbers: No experimental numbers; a review.
limits: EIG values reduced uncertainty, not improved payoff. EIG and EVPI-style value agree only when the payoff depends on the uncertainty being reduced.
agent_relevance: Use EIG only to rank tests; use an EVPI-type bound to decide whether to test at all.

source: Rainforth et al. (2024) estimating EIG is hard
finding: EIG needs a nested expectation. Nested Monte Carlo estimators are biased at any finite inner sample size, because a nonlinear map of unbiased estimates is biased. Fixes include debiasing with multilevel Monte Carlo, variational bounds and importance sampling.
numbers: Bias falls as the inner sample size M grows; the nested estimator converges more slowly than ordinary Monte Carlo.
limits: Selected passages of a long review were read, not all of it.
agent_relevance: Estimating a question's value from a few sampled answers is biased and noisy; compare questions using the same sample settings.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-10) Bayesian experimental design
finding: Lindley (1956): with utility equal to the KL divergence of posterior from prior, expected utility equals the mutual information between parameter and observation. Other utilities named: negative variance, experiment cost. Reviews: Chaloner and Verdinelli (1995), DasGupta (1996).
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: The page does not cover sequential design or give examples.
agent_relevance: Mutual information is nonnegative, so ranking by EIG never penalises a question for being costly; add a cost term.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (arXiv 2410.05563 v3)
finding: Uses the value of computation (VOC) of Russell and Wefald: the expected gain in the best action's value after a computation, minus its cost. Turns it into a reward for chain of thought: log p(y|z,x) - log p(y|x), minus a per-token cost. Trained with expert iteration (RaM).
numbers: VOC(c,b) = E[max_a E[U(a)|b'] - max_a E[U(a)|b]] - cost(c). Reward R = U(z|x,y) - C(z), with C(z) proportional to chain length.
limits: Needs the target answer to score a chain, so it trains only on verifiable data. Models: Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B.
agent_relevance: Shows a value-minus-cost term can be put on thinking length. Our agent would apply it in code at run time, not by training.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2025) RaM results
finding: Compared with STaR and few-shot chain of thought, RaM kept or raised accuracy while using fewer reasoning tokens, and it cut more on easy items than on hard ones.
numbers: 23-32% fewer output tokens than STaR; 35-42% fewer than few-shot prompting; 23-42% overall. Easy versus hard split: length reduction up to 50.3% on Llama-3.2-3B. Out of domain (MMLU-CF): 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR at similar accuracy. One table row pair: RaM 63.5% with 146.2 output tokens versus STaR 61.9% with 215.1.
limits: The row-to-model mapping in the extracted table was ambiguous, so the row pair is indicative only. The easy/hard split is defined by whether direct few-shot answered correctly. Physics and engineering subjects show smaller savings. The paper cites Sprague et al. (2024): explicit chains help mainly on math and logic.
agent_relevance: Per-token cost makes models think less on easy items. Supports an S0 gate that skips thinking when expected value is low.

source: Hu, Liu, Feng, Zhao, Ng, Luu, He, Koh, Hooi (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (arXiv 2402.03271)
finding: UoT simulates future question and answer branches, scores each question by expected information gain over the live candidate set, propagates reward up the tree, and asks the best question. The reward is scaled so it stays in [0,1] and peaks when yes and no are equally likely.
numbers: Binary split: IG = -pA log pA - pN log pN. Simulation depth limited to 3 for budget reasons. Datasets: 20 Questions (Common, Thing), DX, MedDG, FloDial.
limits: The reward has no cost term and treats all questions as equally priced. It is information gain, not improvement in decision value.
agent_relevance: A working recipe for asking the question that splits the live hypotheses in half. Can be coded for the agent's test choice (S4).

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT headline results
finding: UoT raised success rate over direct prompting across five datasets and five models, and shortened conversations.
numbers: Average +38.1% success rate over direct prompting (5 datasets, 5 LLMs); +46.6% for Llama3-70B; beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, original ToT by 28.3%, adapted ToT by 12.4%. GPT-4 closed set: DX 97.0%, MedDG 88.0%, FloDial 67.3% (direct prompting 43.7% on FloDial). DX mean successful conversation length 2.0 versus 3.5 and 3.0 for direct prompting.
limits: The 38.1% is the authors' averaged improvement across settings; t-tests in their Appendix H were not re-checked. The answerer is simulated by GPT-4; 10% of its answers were checked.
agent_relevance: Large gains from information-driven question choice. Supports using an explicit gain score to pick tests.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT per-model results (Table 1)
finding: Gains differ by model, dataset and setting. Closed-set settings (candidate list given) tend to show larger gains.
numbers: Gemini-1.5-Pro MedDG closed set: 51.4 to 81.4. Claude-3-Opus Common open set: 45.0 to 63.1; closed set 52.3 to 66.7. Llama3-70B FloDial closed set: 28.8 to 47.1.
limits: One run per cell as reported; no confidence intervals in the table.
agent_relevance: Expect the biggest gains when the hypothesis set is explicit; keep an explicit candidate list in S4.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT boundary conditions and ablations
finding: Some cells show small or no gain, chain-of-thought and planning prompts can hurt, and the reward-propagation scheme matters.
numbers: Mistral-Large Thing open set 12.5 to 15.0; Llama3-70B Common open set 34.2 to 36.9; DX with GPT-3.5 is 92.1 under all three propagation schemes. GPT-4, UoT versus UoT-Max (20Q-BIG/Common/DX/MedDG/FloDial): 79.3/71.2/97.0/88.0/67.3 versus 79.3/63.7/95.1/83.1/62.6. At about 4.5k tokens (20Q/MD/TB): CoT-SC 32.6/37.6/42.5, adapted ToT 33.8/85.1/60.3, pruned UoT 48.1/88.4/63.2. The text says CoT and PP are worse than plain GPT-4 on 20 Questions.
limits: Open-set gains are modest. Per-cell noise is not given.
agent_relevance: Keep a pruned tree; do not wrap generic chain of thought around the test-choice step.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship (CogSci 2024)
finding: Sample k questions from an LLM, translate each into a program, compute EIG on the board, keep the best. This Monte Carlo choice by EIG gave questions as good as or better than the average human question.
numbers: EIG(x) = H(s) - sum_y p(y|x) H(s|x,y), in bits. Human mean EIG 1.27, best human 3.61, 97% of human questions informative (EIG>0), 18 boards. Single LLM samples averaged 0.65-0.66 for GPT-4 few-shot and CodeLlama; grammar baseline 0.36. At k=5 LLMs near the human mean; at k=10 both beat it (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4 few-shot).
limits: One game domain with an exact world model, so EIG is computable. Still below the best 10-20% of human questions at k=50.
agent_relevance: Sample, score by an exact information measure, pick the best, with a small k. Matches guardrail G5 (code selects).

source: Grand et al. (2024) LIPS grounding failures
finding: LLM-only baselines do not ground questions in the board. Giving GPT-4V the board image did not help. Many sampled questions fail to parse or carry no information.
numbers: Valid-program rate 75% (CodeLlama) and 88% (GPT-4); about 40% (CodeLlama) and 33% (GPT-4) of sampled programs had EIG=0. GPT-4V visual input gave no gain over text only.
limits: Percentages read from the paper text; table cells were partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Filter zero-information candidate tests in code before ranking; the model cannot be trusted to see that a test is useless.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE; arXiv 2310.11589)
finding: Letting the LM ask yes/no questions, open questions or edge cases (generative active task elicitation) gave preference information as good as or better than user-written prompts or labelled examples, with less user effort.
numbers: 388 participants, 3 domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning). GATE beat user prompts in 6 of 10 settings (absolute) and 7 of 10 (area under the p(correct)-time curve). Generative yes/no questions beat prompts in every setting. Mean entropy of p(yes) across questions was 0.77 bits.
limits: Significance against baselines only in content recommendation and email; moral reasoning underpowered. In email only generative active learning beat no-elicitation significantly. Value is measured as predictive gain, not payoff.
agent_relevance: A model that asks can beat a person who must describe everything; asking should cost the asker little effort.

source: Handa, Gal, Pavlick, Goodman, Andreas, Tamkin, Li (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN; arXiv 2403.05534)
finding: OPEN uses Bayesian optimal experimental design to choose the query with the highest expected information gain, and an LM only to extract features and word the question. It outperformed LM-only and design-only elicitation in user studies.
numbers: Metric: Time-Integrated Delta Accuracy. About 39-48 users per condition (48, 44 and 39 in listed conditions). When users had to map features themselves they became significantly worse at stating preferences.
limits: Exact TIDA values are in a figure and were not read. LM-only pairwise questions without a feature set did not probe feature weights, and the chatbot repeated questions in some transcripts.
agent_relevance: Split the roles: code picks the question by information gain, the model only words it. Same split as our program/model rule.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design over the space of possible solutions, not the space of questions. Sample solutions, group them, estimate each question's EIG, ask the best. The stated utility is U(q) = EIG(q) - c(q), a value-minus-cost rule.
numbers: Max EIG for n answer options is log n; a yes/no question reaches 1 bit at an equal split. Compared EIG-uniform, EIG-logprobs, implicit and implicit-ToT. Tasks: 20 Questions (500-animal list), HumanEval (48 tasks) and APPS (47 tasks), 3 run and 3 evaluation seeds.
limits: Several extra LLM calls per question. Tasks filtered to those not already solved at 100%. The cost term c(q) is in the utility but the experiments rank by EIG. Oracle answers are simulated.
agent_relevance: An explicit net-value rule for questions: expected information gain minus cost. Moves the reasoning from questions to the solution space.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) code accuracy by round
finding: Asking by estimated EIG raised accuracy over the model's own question choice, most for weaker models, and open questions beat binary ones.
numbers: HumanEval after 4 rounds: GPT-3.5-turbo binary 70.8 to 85.6 with EIG, open 75.9 to 85.0; Llama3-70B binary 78.8 to 87.5; Llama3-8B open 64.8 to 75.5. APPS round 4: GPT-4o-mini open 75.1 to 87.2; GPT-3.5 binary 62.4 to 71.3. Round 0 is the same across arms (GPT-3.5: 44.1 vs 44.6).
limits: Standard errors are about 1.4-2.6 points on HumanEval and up to 5 on Llama3-8B APPS.
agent_relevance: Gains of 8-15 points after a few clarifying rounds: evidence that ranking tests by information gain beats model-chosen tests.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) boundary: stronger model, smaller gain
finding: With a stronger model and binary questions the EIG advantage is small or absent early.
numbers: HumanEval GPT-4o-mini binary: round 0 base 71.0 vs EIG 69.6; round 1 74.6 vs 73.6; round 4 79.6 vs 81.5 (gap 1.9, standard errors about 2.0). GPT-3.5 gap at round 4 is 14.8 points.
limits: The 20 Questions rank table has a mixed pattern; the direction of its rank scale was not verified, so no claim is drawn from it.
agent_relevance: The value of explicit information scoring shrinks as the model already asks well; measure on our own data before trusting a gain.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning (arXiv 2402.06025)
finding: Sequential Monte Carlo over natural-language rules. The LLM proposes experiments and rules, and an information-gain score reranks the proposed experiments. It beat a ReAct-style baseline and batch inference with refinement on Zendo and ActiveACRE and fit human data.
numbers: Zendo: humans 5.26/8, ReAct-style agent 4.60/8, best model 6.55/8, fuzzy-rule variant 5.35/8. Human-data log-likelihood: best model -1478.82 (online, fuzzy) versus -1539 for the earlier best model. Replacing InfoGain with LLM-only or random experiments significantly degraded performance.
limits: Table 3 values for the three experiment proposers were not recovered in the text extract; the direction (InfoGain best) is the authors' statement. Human-model fit is an inverted U in compute budget.
agent_relevance: LLM-proposed tests need an information-gain rerank; an LLM alone does not pick tests as well. Too much compute also hurts.

source: Ren, Dixit, Bodrova, Singh, Tu, Brown et al. (2023) Robots That Ask For Help: KnowNo (arXiv 2307.01928)
finding: Conformal prediction turns LLM option probabilities into prediction sets with a coverage guarantee. The robot acts when the set has one option and asks a human otherwise. It hits a target success rate while asking less than baselines.
numbers: Target failure level epsilon=0.15 in the main comparison. Human help reduced by 10-24% against baselines, up to 24% against Simple Set in the most ambiguous scenarios.
limits: The guarantee needs exchangeable calibration data; in multi-step planning the i.i.d. assumption fails and a sequence-level bound is used. This is a calibrated ask-or-act rule, not an explicit value-of-information calculation.
agent_relevance: A practical ask-or-act gate: ask only when the plausible set is not a single answer, with the threshold calibrated on held-out data.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv 2505.06120)
finding: When instructions arrive over several turns, models often answer early on assumptions instead of asking, then rely on that early answer. Average performance fell 39% across six generation tasks compared with fully specified single-turn prompts.
numbers: -39% average; 15 LLMs; 200,000+ simulated conversations; N=10 simulations per model and condition.
quote: prematurely attempt to generate final solutions
limits: Tests under-specification without measuring whether a better asking rule would fix it.
agent_relevance: Models do not weigh the value of one more question before answering; the scaffold must force an ask-or-answer decision.
